title_original: Explore the World of Avant-Garde Pioneers Nathaniel Dorsky and Jerome Hiler in Exclusive Trailer for Illuminations
editorial_title_zh: 在《Illuminations》独家预告片中探索前卫先锋纳撒尼尔·多尔斯基与杰罗姆·希勒的世界
editorial_excerpt_zh: 一对前卫电影先锋终于迎来了实至名归的纪录片肖像。纳撒尼尔·多尔斯基（Nathaniel Dorsky）与杰罗姆·希勒（Jerome Hiler）两人共同的艺术与奉献实践已延续了六十多年，他们正是帕特里克·申（Patrick Shen）与布兰登·维德（Brandon Vedder）沉思式作品的主角……

article_text:
A pair of avant-garde pioneers are finally getting a much-deserved documentary portrait. Nathaniel Dorsky and Jerome Hiler, whose shared artistic and devotional practice has endured for more than sixty years, are the subjects of Patrick Shen and Brandon Vedder’s contemplative portrait Illuminations .

After for a world premiere at DOC NYC on November 11 at the IFC Center and November 13 at Village East by Angelika, Anthology Film Archives will present three programs, all on 16mm, devoted to the work of Dorsky and Hiler from November 16-18. Ahead of said premiere, we’re thrilled to debut the first trailer.

Here’s the synopsis: “Working exclusively with silent 16mm film, Dorsky and Hiler have devoted their lives to a cinema of attention, light, perception, and presence. I lluminations traces their journey from the underground film culture of the 1960s to major retrospectives at the Museum of Modern Art, while exploring a larger question at the heart of their work: Can cinema become not simply an art form, but a wisdom form—a way of teaching us how to see?”

“Illuminations traces the artists’ intertwined lives from the underground film culture of 1960s New York and San Francisco through decades of largely private screenings and artistic practice to major retrospectives and sold-out programs at institutions including the Museum of Modern Art,” the synopsis continues. “Along the way, the film considers Dorsky and Hiler’s belief in cinema’s capacity to alter perception—to restore a sense of wonder to the ordinary and, in Dorsky’s formulation, to become a kind of ‘wisdom form.'”

See the trailer and poster below.

title_original: The Netflix Original Movie Experiment Has Failed — and Netflix Will Be All the Better for It
editorial_title_zh: 网飞的原创电影实验已经失败——而网飞也将因此变得更好
editorial_excerpt_zh: 网飞在过去10年里一直试图让电影院变得过时。现在，该公司正在放弃这一尝试，恰好来得及避免让自己也变得过时。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "2025年4月，不知何故仿佛就在18个月前，网飞联席CEO泰德·萨兰多斯（Ted Sarandos）参加了一场公开对话，对话以《时代》杂志主编向他提出一个简单问题开始：“你们毁了好莱坞吗？”这本意是一个俏皮的破冰提问，而萨兰多斯脸上掠过一丝坏笑，给出了符合其财富和权力的颠覆者身份的预期回答：“不，我们在拯救好莱坞。”", "links": [{"text": "Netflix", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/netflix/"}, {"text": "Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation", "url": "https://variety.com/2025/film/news/netflix-ceo-ted-sarandos-movie-theaters-outdated-1236376565/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他们正在拯救好莱坞，使其免于它之所以存在的根本原因，以及它之所以——也是唯一的原因——能够继续对集体想象力施加无与伦比的、不成比例影响的原因：电影院。“我们正处于一个过渡期，”萨兰多斯随后在小组讨论中详述道，“人们在成长过程中会想：‘我想在大得惊人的银幕上拍电影，让陌生人观看它们，[并让它们]在影院里上映两个月，人们会哭泣，门票售罄’……这是一个过时的概念。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MCDFOOR_EC009.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "《发条橙》", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-29-at-12.39.59-PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "《沙丘3》爆米花桶", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "切至：2026年10月。好莱坞正处于比以往任何时候都更加岌岌可危的状态，而网飞刚刚租下了纽约最大的AMC影院，为该公司有史以来最关键的电影举办了一场预告片首映礼。在这场活动中，“纳尼亚”导演格蕾塔·格韦格（Greta Gerwig）在巨大的IMAX银幕前接受了斯蒂芬·科尔伯特（Stephen Colbert）的采访，现场记者观众们则嚼着糖果和爆米花。银幕巨大无比。格韦格哭了。当《纳尼亚传奇：外甥的魔法师》（Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew）于明年2月在影院上映时，它将在那里独家上映（近）两个月，之后才能在网飞上观看。萨兰多斯有一点说得对：我们正处于过渡期。只是这并不是他脑海中想的那种过渡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自从网飞在2015年通过《无境之兽》（Beasts of No Nation）进军直接上线流媒体的电影领域以来，他们的最终目标——既未明说却又毋庸置疑——就是彻底消灭电影院。他们成为了第一家转型为好莱坞大制片厂的内容分发服务商，随后又成为第一家试图将好莱坞转型为内容分发服务商的好莱坞大制片厂。100多年来，电影产业一直依赖于出售电影票；网飞的议程则是切断中间商，让订阅该服务变得像拥有一部智能手机一样不可或缺。他们甚至在这一过程中买下了一些历史悠久的影院，以使这个过程尽可能平稳温和。", "links": [{"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "网飞之所以那样运作，并不是因为他们比其他任何电影公司都更邪恶（甚至连萨兰多斯也没有狂妄到在这方面去跟大卫·扎斯拉夫（David Zaslav）和埃利森（Ellison）竞争）——他们那样运作是因为他们是一家科技公司，涉足电影制片厂只是权宜之计。而且，当科技公司离艺术太近时，它们总有一种滑稽的方式，表现得像四维空间的殖民者。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如果你的业务是制造人们想看的东西，你的首要任务就是制作电影——理想情况下（但并不常见）是好电影——并在大型礼堂中放映它们，让顾客支付适度的费用，以原本应有的方式体验它们。如果你的业务是向人们兜售一个他们可能并不想看到的未来，你的首要任务就是让现在显得过时。现在可以在一秒钟内变成过去，但需要数十亿美元来让这个过程看起来比实际应有的更慢。在现在的大限到来之前，让它显得毫无价值、令人嫌弃。说服人们它不仅在流逝，而且还在拖他们的后腿。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "萨兰多斯可能是一个终身影迷，网飞最初也是因为他在电影发行方面的深厚背景而将其招致麾下，但毫无疑问，他现在已经是一个科技大佬了。我其实不能因此责怪他。这家伙既是他所处时代的产物，也是其时代的象征，尽管我很难想到还有哪个制片厂高管曾如此常规地让我的热血沸腾，但我猜，如果达里尔·F·扎努克（Darryl F. Zanuck）和路易斯·B·梅耶（Louis B. Mayer）被委任去衡量“观看时长”并与野兽先生（Mr. Beast）争夺我们的注意力时，他们也会喷出同样的一堆废话。科技大佬们就是得这么说话。他们的商业模式、股价和企业神秘感要求他们表现得像来自明日世界的奇异使者——面带微笑、随性自在，但一心想要摧毁实现其未来愿景所需的一切代价。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这就是为什么网飞只在不得不遵守的范围内遵守好莱坞的规则，即使坚持其核心指令意味着将唾手可得的真金白银拱手让人。他们将“电影”放入“影院”是为了获得奖项资格，并防止才华横溢的创作者们放火烧公司的服务器农场。但即便在大牌导演恳求更长的院线窗口期时——甚至在有明显的公众对此类事物有需求时，比如2022年的《利刃出鞘：抽丝剥茧》（Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery）那样的著名案例——网飞在电影票销售中本可赚得的数百万美元，与他们通过让电影票概念过时而有望获得的数十亿美元相比，也根本不值一提。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/glass-onion.webp?w=650", "alt": "", "caption": "《利刃出鞘：抽丝剥茧》", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一些电影人拿到了大笔资金，交出了他们的内容，并带着尊严全身而退。另一些人则开心地饮下迷魂汤，拥抱了一个满足观众不再是等式一部分的、以订阅为驱动的未来。正如乔·鲁索（Joe Russo）在宣传2022年每个人最喜爱、最让人印象深刻的电影《灰影人》（The Gray Man）时所说：“这种认为影院是神圣空间的观点简直是狗屁。”这倒也说得过去——如果我知道自己即将执导《电幻国度》（The Electric State），我大概也会忍不住喋喋不休地抱怨人们必须在公共场合看电影是多么糟糕的一件事，因为在公共场合大家的预期是你要安坐全场，甚至可能还会享受其中。这太野蛮了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁索还进一步贬低了观影体验的“精英主义”，呼应或预见了萨兰多斯此前的论点，即全国各地的许多人已不再能轻易去到多厅影院。我们都在寻找那个始作俑者，但他的观点依然成立。我永远不会忘记，自始至终直言不讳地支持网飞议程的阿瓦·杜威内（Ava DuVernay），唯有说服迪士尼在当地社区中心内搭建一家临时影院，才能在她那没有电影院的家乡康普顿（Compton）放映《时间的皱折》（A Wrinkle in Time）。让网飞去解决电影院短缺或分布不均的问题，他们的解决方案大概会让所有电影院（至少是他们不拥有的那些）全都倒闭。", "links": [{"text": "a pop-up cinema", "url": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In April 2025, somehow only 18 months ago, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation that began with Time magazine’s editor-in-chief asking him a simple question: “Have you destroyed Hollywood?” It was meant as a cheeky icebreaker, and Sarandos — a smirk cracking across his face — gave the exact response you would expect from a disruptor of his wealth and power: “No, we’re saving Hollywood.”", "links": [{"text": "Netflix", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/netflix/"}, {"text": "Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation", "url": "https://variety.com/2025/film/news/netflix-ceo-ted-sarandos-movie-theaters-outdated-1236376565/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "They were saving Hollywood from the very reason it exists in the first place, and the reason — the only reason — why it continues to exert a peerlessly disproportionate influence on the collective imagination: movie theaters. “We’re in a period of transition,” Sarandos elaborated later in the panel. “Folks grew up thinking, ‘I want to make movies on a gigantic screen and have strangers watch them [and to have them] play in the theater for two months and people cry and sold-out shows’ …It’s an outdated concept.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MCDFOOR_EC009.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "'A Clockwork Orange'", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-29-at-12.39.59-PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Dune 3 Popcorn Bucket", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cut to: October 2026. For more than 100 years, the film industry depended on selling movie tickets; Netflix’s agenda was to cut out the middleman and make subscribing to the service feel as obligatory as owning a smartphone. And tech companies have a funny way of acting like fourth-dimensional colonizers whenever they get too close to the arts."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If your business is to make things that people want to see, your top priority is to produce movies — ideally but infrequently good movies — and project them in large auditoriums where customers can pay a modest fee to experience them as they were meant to be seen. article_text:
In April 2025, somehow only 18 months ago, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos participated in a public conversation that began with Time magazine’s editor-in-chief asking him a simple question: “Have you destroyed Hollywood?” It was meant as a cheeky icebreaker, and Sarandos — a smirk cracking across his face — gave the exact response you would expect from a disruptor of his wealth and power: “No, we’re saving Hollywood.”

They were saving Hollywood from the very reason it exists in the first place, and the reason — the only reason — why it continues to exert a peerlessly disproportionate influence on the collective imagination: movie theaters. “We’re in a period of transition,” Sarandos elaborated later in the panel. “Folks grew up thinking, ‘I want to make movies on a gigantic screen and have strangers watch them [and to have them] play in the theater for two months and people cry and sold-out shows’ …It’s an outdated concept.”

Cut to: October 2026. Hollywood is in a more precarious state than ever, and Netflix just rented out New York’s biggest AMC to stage a trailer premiere for the most crucial movie the company has ever made, an event where “Narnia” director Greta Gerwig was interviewed by Stephen Colbert in front of a massive IMAX screen as an audience of journalists munched on candy and popcorn. The screen was gigantic. Gerwig cried. When “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” opens in theaters next February, it will play there exclusively for (almost) two months before it’s available to watch on Netflix. Sarandos was right about one thing: We are in a period of transition. It’s just not the transition he had in mind.

Ever since Netflix entered the straight-to-streaming film space with “Beasts of No Nation” back in 2015, their ultimate goal — as unstated as it is unambiguous — has been nothing less than the complete elimination of movie theaters. They became the first content delivery service to transform into a major Hollywood studio, and then the first major Hollywood studio to try to transform Hollywood into a content delivery service. For more than 100 years, the film industry depended on selling movie tickets; Netflix’s agenda was to cut out the middleman and make subscribing to the service feel as obligatory as owning a smartphone. They even bought a few historic theaters along the way to make the process as smooth and gentle as possible.

Netflix didn’t operate that way because they’re more evil than any of the other movie studios (not even Sarandos has the hubris required to compete with Davids Zaslav and Ellison in that regard) — they operated that way because they’re a tech company that only became a movie studio as a means to an end. And tech companies have a funny way of acting like fourth-dimensional colonizers whenever they get too close to the arts.

If your business is to make things that people want to see, your top priority is to produce movies — ideally but infrequently good movies — and project them in large auditoriums where customers can pay a modest fee to experience them as they were meant to be seen. If your business is to sell people on a future they may not want to see, your top priority is to make the present seem obsolete. The present can become the past in a second, but it takes billions of dollars to make that process feel slower than it should. To make the present feel worthless and unwanted before its time is up. To convince people that it isn’t just passing by, but also holding them back.

Sarandos might be a lifelong cinephile whom Netflix originally hired for his deep background in film distribution, but there’s no doubt he’s a tech bro now. I can’t really blame him for that. The guy is both a product and an emblem of his times, and though I’m hard-pressed to think of another studio executive who’s ever made my blood run hotter on such a regular basis, I suspect that the likes of Darryl F. Zanuck and Louis B. Mayer would’ve spouted all the same bullshit had they been tasked with measuring “view hours” and competing against Mr. Beast for our attention. That’s just how tech bros have to talk. Their business models, stock prices, and corporate mystiques require them to act like weird ambassadors from the world of tomorrow — smiling and casual but always bent on destroying whatever it takes to bring their vision of the future to bear.

This is why Netflix has played by Hollywood’s rules only as much as it had to, even when sticking to its prime directive meant leaving free money on the table. They put “movies” into “theaters” to qualify them for awards and keep talent from setting the company’s server farms on fire. But even when major directors pleaded for longer windows — and even when there was a clear public demand for the same thing, as was famously the case with “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery” in 2022 — the millions Netflix might have earned in movie ticket sales were no match for the billions they stood to gain from rendering the concept of movie tickets obsolete.

Some filmmakers got the bag, delivered their content, and escaped with their dignity intact. Others happily gulped down the Kool-Aid and embraced a subscription-driven future where satisfying audiences was no longer part of the equation. As Joe Russo put it while promoting “The Gray Man,” everyone’s favorite and most well-remembered film of 2022: “This idea that the theater is a sacred space is bullshit.” Fair enough — if I knew I was about to direct “The Electric State,” I probably wouldn’t be able to shut up about how awful it is that people have to watch movies in public, where the expectation is they’ll sit through the entire thing and maybe even enjoy themselves. It’s barbaric.

Russo also went on to decry the “elitism” of the theatrical experience, echoing — or anticipating — Sarandos’ argument that many people across the country can’t easily get to a multiplex anymore. We’re all trying to find the guy who did that, but the point stands. I will never forget that Ava DuVernay, an outspoken advocate of Netflix’s agenda from the beginning, could only screen “A Wrinkle in Time” in her theater-less hometown of Compton because she convinced Disney to build a pop-up cinema inside a local community center. Ask Netflix to address the lack/uneven distribution of movie theaters, and their solution would be to put them all out of business (all of the ones they don’t own, anyway).

Netflix’s throw-out-the-baby-with-the-bathwater approach hinged on the presumption that people would happily forfeit the possibility of enjoying a proper theatrical experience in exchange for the promise of being able to enjoy “ Bright ” at home. Like all such acts of mass enshittification, that pivot was sold to the public as progress — as part of a devil’s bargain that sacrificed creativity at the altar of convenience. And, like all such acts of mass enshittification, it was made possible by the fact that the system it was meant to supplant had grown complacent. It’s hard to defend the Union Square Regal as a holy temple of the arts when 10 of its screens are playing Guy Ritchie’s live-action remake of “Aladdin” or whatever.

Of course, that was a blockbuster from the before times, and the COVID pandemic only further empowered Netflix to fulfill its mission. Not only were multiplexes shuttered for months (or years) on end, but the legacy studios fell over themselves to help their streaming rivals make semi-permanent inroads with the public. If parties had been safe to host in December 2020, Netflix would surely have thrown a generational rager to celebrate Warner Bros.’ decision to release “Dune,” “The Suicide Squad,” and 15 other major titles directly to HBO Max. Even as the pandemic began to subside and “Top Gun: Maverick” took flight at the box office two summers later, it seemed as if movie theaters — and the culture that sustained them — would never truly recover from such an unprecedented self-devaluation of corporate assets.

But then a funny thing happened: People kept going to the movies. In fits and starts at first, and then more regularly. In 2023, monocultural events like “Barbenheimer” had to be hyped and telegraphed months in advance before they reached critical mass. By the fall of 2026, a three-hour documentary about a blonde fraudster could become a nationally sold-out sensation with less than five weeks of lead time (although Elizabeth Holmes would argue, of course, that it always could have done that). Altogether, this year’s domestic box office is on track to reach $10 billion, almost matching the numbers from 2019.

There are a number of reasons for that, but I think this is the biggest one: As soon as screens reopened, the movies as a medium were immediately redefined by the ability to experience them in theaters. In an article published almost 10 years ago on this very website, I asked, “When you watch something on Netflix, are you watching a movie, or are you having a movie-like experience?” It was a question prompted by the dawning realization that “film” was becoming something of a misnomer in a world where content was classified less by the nature of its production than by the mechanism of its distribution — and by the gnawing sense that movies weren’t really being seen on Netflix, even on the off chance that someone was actually able to find a good one to watch on the service.

Since then, Netflix has doubled and quadrupled down on the bet that people wouldn’t sweat the difference between algorithmic streaming content and traditional studio fare. Between movies that had been made to satisfy a data point, and movies that had benefited from — or at least been put through — a more elaborate development process. The company hasn’t been completely immune to producing good films, and they’ve certainly spent a lot of money to acquire a variety of great ones (for every “Emilia Pérez” there’s at least one “May December” and several must-see documentaries), but unadvertised vanity runs did little to distinguish masterpieces like “Power of the Dog” from starry imitation slop like “The Adam Project,” and lower-profile gems like “They Cloned Tyrone” and “The World Is Yours” were practically guaranteed to be lost in the shuffle.

Meanwhile, the more determined Netflix became to mimic Hollywood entertainment at home, the further they widened the self-evident perception gap between DTV junk and IMAX-worthy spectacle. “Red Notice” may have been “viewed” by every person on Earth, but nobody remembers watching it. The difference between that and a similarly putrid theatrical release with one of the same stars (let’s go with “Black Adam”) is the difference between scrolling across a funny meme on your phone (face blank and eyes dead as you retweet it with the caption “lol stop I’m fucking DECEASED”) and enjoying a lived experience that has the chance to be remembered by virtue of its shared and unimpeachable reality. To quote Jia Tolentino’s “Trick Mirror,” the more difficult the 21st century makes it to “differentiate between the pretext for an experience, the record of that experience, and the experience itself,” the deeper that movie theaters will become reingrained as a determinative element of the movies themselves. The more difficult AI makes it to differentiate between slop and spectacle, the more people will unconsciously privilege the legitimacy a proper release confers, even on the biggest pieces of shit.

They call it “effort-signaling,” the way labor becomes “an integral character to the point where the final product ends up being a secondary concern.” And by “they,” I, of course, mean “ a tweet that I saw while I was writing this article. ” Releasing a movie — even a bad movie — requires effort. The future that Ted Sarandos has brought to us (and us to) with the inflexible weight of a destiny is, to his great consternation, a future where people will only be willing to invest themselves in things that someone else has credibly invested themselves in first.

It’s no wonder that Netflix’s streaming competitors have suffered from similar woes in this space. “F1” and “Killers of the Flower Moon” did major numbers at home on the backs of robust theatrical rollouts, while most movies that went straight to Apple TV barely seem to exist. Remember the Justin Timberlake vehicle “Palmer”? Apparently I wrote like 1,200 words about it. What about “Wolfs,” the George Clooney/Brad Pitt/Austin Abrams action-comedy that pivoted away from a wide release less than six weeks before it came out, immediately became Apple TV’s most-viewed film ever, and then sank into the bottomless abyss of lost media just as fast? Not lost , I suppose, but hiding in plain sight.

It’s likewise no wonder that the one Netflix movie that blossomed into a bona fide sensation, of the roughly 4,000 original films they’ve released since 2015, was 1.) produced outside the company, 2.) clearly excellent, and 3.) squarely targeted at children who could obsess over it with their friends all summer long and inhabit its characters through dress-up and singing. “K-Pop Demon Hunters” was a perfect vessel for the kind of engagement Netflix’s entire business model exists to diminish, and I suspect its success was a wake-up call — or at least an early warning sign — that Netflix desperately needed to be saved from itself.

To the company’s sincere credit, they’ve recently made strides towards that end. Netflix’s org chart might be in crisis, and its subscribers are growing increasingly restless about the awful cadence of content worth caring about. But the inevitable pivot toward real theatrical releases will meaningfully raise the profile of their exclusive film titles in the coming months, even if few of them perform as well as “La Bola Negra” has so far .

That pivot represents a rare about-face for a tech giant that has sought to remake the world in its own image, consumer happiness be damned. In the same interview where Sarandos called movie theaters an outdated concept, he also insisted that “Netflix is a very consumer-focused company,” and that “we really do care that we deliver the program to you in a way you want to watch it.” At long last, they seem to have figured out which way that might be.
excerpt_original: Netflix spent the last 10 years trying to render movie theaters obsolete. Now the company is giving up just in time to avoid becoming obsolete itself.

article_text:
Forget about going to the cottage. “ Heated Rivalry ” fans will be going to movie theaters in November.

Almost a year after the queer hockey romance series premiered in the U.S., Regal will release all six episodes in more than 650 theaters nationwide for a limited run Nov. 6-30.

“When a series connects with audiences the way ‘Heated Rivalry’ has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” Brooks LeBoeuf, senior vice president of U.S. content at Regal, said in a statement Thursday. “Nearly a year after its premiere, we’re proud to work with our partners to turn a season fans have watched again and again into a true theatrical event. It’s a chance to celebrate the story, its creators and its performances before Season 2 arrives in 2027.”

Related Stories

'Sea of Glass' Brings 'Country Gothic Noir' Tradition to Greece With Story of Two Women Finding Solidarity Across Generations

Tribeca Prizewinner Darko Lungulov Wraps Production on Serbian Coming-of-Age Drama ‘1970’: 'It Is a Story About Today' (EXCLUSIVE)

Based on Rachel Reid ’s bestselling novels, “Heated Rivalry” follows rival hockey players Shane Hollander ( Hudson Williams ) and Ilya Rozanov ( Connor Storrie ) as they secretly fall in love. The series quickly became a global hit, with Williams and Storrie becoming two of Hollywood’s most sought-after actors. Written and directed by Jacob Tierney, “Heated Rivalry,” currently in production of its second season, also features François Arnaud , Robbie G.K. , Christina Chang , Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova, Sophie Nélisse and Dylan Walsh.

During the theatrical run, which Regal is leading in partnership with Sphere Abacus, moviegoers can revisit the series in order across three paired screenings: Episodes 1 and 2 (“Rookies” and “Olympians”), Episodes 3 and 4 (“Hunter” and “Rose”), and Episodes 5 and 6 (“I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”). Tickets for each pairing cost $9.99.

“‘Heated Rivalry’ is a global phenomenon creating a rush of social media and press activity wherever it lands,” said Hana Palmer, executive director, global distribution and partnerships at Sphere Abacus. “We’re very excited to give audiences the opportunity to watch the drama unfold on big screens in North America, the U.K., Australia and New Zealand.”

Regal screenings will also feature welcome content from the series’ cast and director, while participating locations will offer limited-time themed cocktails: Summer in Montreal and Russians Don’t Blush. In-theater marketing support is provided by PaperAirplane.

Advance tickets for “Heated Rivalry” are available now at theater box offices, on mobile apps and through REGmovies.com .

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Laysla De Oliveira , star of Paramount+’s Lioness , and Italian actor Riccardo Scamarcio ( A Haunting in Venice ) have wrapped on Telephone , an indie sci-fi thriller directed by Anthony Scott Burns.

Shot in Sudbury, Ontario, with The Walking Dead ‘s Gale Anne Hurd among its EPs, Telephone follows Sandy, who is abducted by her mysterious neighbors and told she must travel back in time to save the future. Once in the past, she faces a choice: trust these strangers for the sake of mankind or follow another traveler who offers to help her prevent the tragedy that shaped her life.

Related Stories

May El-Toukhy's 'Woman Unknown' Wins Golden Lion For Best Film At Venice Film Festival - Full Winners List

Audible Teases Jonathan Bailey's "Seductive" Performance In 'Dracula' At Venice Preview Of Ambitious Multilingual Adaptation

Hailing from Valhalla Entertainment, Beyond the Frame and 10.80 Films, the film also stars Rohan Campbell ( The Monkey ), Tenika Davis ( Spartacus: House of Ashur ) and Michael Greyeyes ( Blood Quantum ).

Watch on Deadline

Script is by Jack Stanley, with revisions by Burns. The film is produced by Jason Ross Jallet, Andrew Bronfman, Jonathan Bronfman and Benoit Roland, with Hurd, Todd Brown, Jack Stanley and Phillip Kobylanski as executive producers.

Hurd told Deadline: “Not only were we blessed with a fantastic cast on Telephone , but our director, Anthony Scott Burns, is an incredible talent. His vision for the film is apparent in every frame and, having worked with some of the world’s top directors, I can absolutely see him joining their ranks.”

Earlier this month, Brazilian-Canadian actress De Oliveira won the award for Breakthrough Actress – Series at the Critics Choice Association’s Celebración of Cinema & Television. This was for her starring role opposite Zoe Saldaña in Taylor Sheridan’s Lioness . She’s also been seen starring in Netflix’s Locke & Key and is repped by Gersh, Wright Entertainment, and Myman Greenspan.

Scamarcio won Best Actor in the Orizzonti sidebar competition of this year’s Venice Film Festival for his work in the film I Figli Della Scimmia ( Children of the Monkey ). He is repped by Tavistock Wood Management and Plan A.

Burns’ past films include the indies Come True and Our House . He’s earned multiple nominations at the Directors Guild of Canada Awards and is repped by SpectreVision.

Campbell is repped by CAA, Webster Talent Management and Sol22; Davis by Buchwald and Zero Gravity; Greyeyes by TalentWorks, The Arc, and Mills Kaplan Entertainment; and screenwriter Stanley by Silent R Management and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

article_text:
If Michael Douglas had his way, he would’ve left the Marvel Cinematic Universe after starring in 2015’s Ant-Man and its sequel.

In a new interview, the actor got real about his time in the MCU and asked the studio to kill off his character.

“I would have been killed off after the second one, but they wouldn’t let me,” Douglas said on the Happy Sad Confused podcast.

Douglas shared that he wanted to star in a CGI-heavy film, adding, “I said, ‘I’ve never done a green screen movie.’ I [told] all my agents, ‘I’d like to do one of these green screen movies to see what they’re like,’ you know? Because it’s amazing. It’s nothing, just a green screen, and they show you the pictures of what it’s gonna look like when it’s all finished.”

Related Stories

'Smear' Campaign: George Clooney, Betty Gilpin, Adam Scott & Laverne Cox Unite For Midterms Fundraiser Of Clark Gregg Penned Political Play

Amanda Seyfried Explains Turning Down 'Guardians Of The Galaxy' For Family: "Just Not For Me"

After starring in the MCU, Douglas said, “It’s hard acting, man,” adding, “It’s coming at you here, this and that, you know.”

Watch on Deadline

Douglas joked about reading the “fine print” of his contract, saying that Ant-Man star Paul Rudd “was a wonderful actor” and the cast was “a lovely group,” noting, “but then you can’t get out of it.”

After starring in Ant-Man in 2015 as Hank Pym, Douglas would reprise the role on several other occasions. Douglas reprised his role in 2018’s Ant-Man and the Wasp , 2019’s Avengers: Endgame, and 2023’s Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania . He also voiced the character in several episodes of the Disney+ animated series What If…? , between 2021 and 2023.

Watch Michael Douglas’ full interview in the video below.

"paragraph", "text": "英文片名取自罗伯特·弗罗斯特的诗作，陈可辛称这首诗是他人生的座右铭，而中文片名《明天会更好》则字面意为“Tomorrow Will Be Better”。“真的没有所谓的正确路径，”他说。“无论是对是错，全在于你如何走过。路是自己走出来的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“那部电影给了我未来30年的电影生命，直到现在，”陈可辛说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说，90%的人因为那单唯一的一部电影而记住他，“就好像我后来再也没有拍出更好的作品一样”，他称这既是一种祝福，也是一个他想要打破的魔咒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "陈可辛还表示，90年代标志着香港电影衰落的开始，而非其黄金时代。他将自己为梦工厂执导的电影《情书》形容为一次艰难的经历。他说，跨文化工作并没有难倒他，因为他在泰国的华人社区长大，即便在香港也常常觉得自己是个局外人。真正让他感到吃力的是一个企业化系统——在这个系统中，谁说了算并不明确——以及对试映的依赖，他将其比作当年的算法。他说自己可能是在美国制片厂体制内拍非动作片的第一位、若非唯一一位香港电影人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“如果当年我去美国或好莱坞时，能拥有今天我对电影、市场以及如何应对企业体制的认知，我大概会表现得更好，”陈可辛说。“那时候我太年轻，也太天真了。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "后来有观众问他是如何在中国内地的审查制度中游刃有余的，陈可辛回答：“与大企业打交道非常、非常困难。如果我能挺过那一关，我就能挺过任何关。”他补充说，预算、明星、片厂或审查制度的局限往往会促使电影人变得更有创意。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "离开好莱坞后，陈可辛成立了泛亚洲企业 Applause Pictures，在两年半的时间里制作了10部电影，其中大部分是恐怖片。其出品包括《见鬼》系列和恐怖短片合集《三更》，汇聚了朴赞郁、三池崇史、金知云、陈果等导演。他还担任韩国导演许秦豪（新加坡国际电影节开幕影片《刺客》的导演）执导的《春逝》的执行制片人，他十分喜爱许秦豪的处女作《八月照相馆》。但一个原计划与许秦豪和日本岩井俊二合作的三段式爱情故事项目却未能找到投资。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“如果我们继续这种泛亚洲的努力，我这一辈子就只能被困在拍恐怖片里了，”陈可辛在谈到转战中国内地、其内地的第一部作品是2005年歌舞片《如果·爱》时的决定如是说。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "台下一名有志于成为编剧的观众问他如何处理效果不佳的场景。“我通常不会帮他们修改。我会让他们一遍、一遍、又一遍、又一遍地修改，”陈可辛说道，并补充说，虽然他在家里对什么都说“好”，但在对待编剧时可不会这样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他将《投名状》的编剧归功于9位编剧，并透露编剧们开玩笑说，他电影里的编剧们塞不下一辆小巴。“我把编剧榨干到死，然后再榨干另一个编剧，”他说道。“所以编剧圈其实很不怎么喜欢我。但拍电影可不是为了讨人喜欢。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管陈可辛常被视为一位不断转换类型的导演，但他表示，贯穿其作品的核心关切是一致的，他提到了自己导演处女作《双城故事》、《甜蜜蜜》、《如果·爱》甚至《投名状》中的三角恋，他称《投名状》讲述的是三个结拜兄弟之间的三角关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“拍每一部电影，都是在回答我在人生的那个阶段、那个时间点上所拥有的一些关于生活的疑问，”他说道。“所以从某种程度上说，在过去的36年里，我脑子里一直在拍同一部电影。”", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Acclaimed Asian filmmaker Peter Chan Ho-sun , director of “Comrades: Almost a Love Story” and “The Warlords,” said he will probably use AI in his filmmaking but “definitely not AIGC,” or AI-generated content, and that the two-hour feature will hold its ground against short-form and vertical dramas, at least in his lifetime.

Speaking at an In Conversation event at the Singapore International Film Festival , Chan was asked by an audience member whether he had ever doubted his decision to go into the film industry. His advice to aspiring filmmakers: “This is probably the toughest time for film, but do I believe this medium is going to be lost and gone to short-form entertainment? No.”

He said he would probably use AI as a technique, the way the industry already uses CGI and special effects, noting that CGI has relied on AI for years without calling it that. “Anything that helps me make movies, I welcome. But they won’t know art. Movies are still made by people,” Chan said.

Young audiences’ shrinking attention spans have them turning to short and vertical dramas, Chan said, while at the other end, people are listening to podcasts that run for hours, and Christopher Nolan did podcasts around the world to explain his purist approach of making “Oppenheimer” the way movies were made in the ’50s. “So there are two completely opposite ends of the spectrum that are surviving and thriving simultaneously. So I believe that movie will be around for a long, long time,” he told a rapt audience at the Grand Ballroom, Marina Bay Sands.

Chan’s latest film, “The Road Not Taken,” premiered in Toronto. “My new movie is about Alzheimer’s, but it’s really not just about Alzheimer’s. It’s about a broken family that has all sorts of problems a family could have,” he said.

The story centers on a couple in the middle of divorce proceedings when the wife, who has early-onset Alzheimer’s, no longer remembers the divorce and drifts back in her mind to the time they fell in love in their 20s. A harsh grandfather and the couple’s relationship with their Gen Z daughter complete the picture. The daughter in the film is 20, the same age as Chan’s own daughter, who is training to become an actor. Chan’s partner is actor Sandra Ng.

The English title comes from the Robert Frost poem, which Chan called his life motto, while the Chinese title, “Ming Tian Hui Geng Hao,” translates as “Tomorrow Will Be Better.” “There’s really no right path,” he said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, it’s all about how you walk it. You make it right.”

While researching the film, Chan visited an Alzheimer’s care institution in Chengdu, in China’s Sichuan province, where he picked up an eight-word Mandarin phrase that he used to sum up his career: go with the flow, and know when to stop. In the ’90s, when he was making romantic comedies at United Filmmakers Organization (UFO), the company he co-founded, gangster pictures and wuxia ruled Hong Kong screens. “We were not exactly going with the flow, but we did make the flow, somehow,” he said.

That same flow later carried him to “The Warlords,” which he described as his biggest film. “Never had I thought that I would ever make a historical epic battle movie with Jet Li. That was never, ever in my agenda for my entire life,” Chan said.

This year marks the 30th anniversary of “Comrades,” which Chan made at 34 as his seventh feature and which captures Hong Kong between 1985 and 1995. He left Hong Kong on Christmas Eve 1996, and only after returning from America around two and a half years later did he grasp how deeply the film had affected filmmakers in mainland China, South Korea and Southeast Asia, even though, he said, it probably only barely recouped its investment.

“That movie gave me a lease of movie life for the next 30 years, until now,” Chan said.

He said 90% of people remember him for that single film, “as if I have not done better afterwards,” calling it a blessing but also a spell he wanted to break.

Chan, who also said the ’90s marked the start of Hong Kong cinema’s decline rather than its golden age, described his DreamWorks film “The Love Letter” as a difficult experience. He was not thrown by working across cultures, he said, having grown up Thai-Chinese and feeling like an outsider even in Hong Kong. What he struggled with was a corporate system where it was unclear who called the shots, and a reliance on test screenings that he likened to today’s algorithms. He said he was probably the first, if not the only, Hong Kong filmmaker to make a non-action film inside the U.S. studio system.

“Had I gone to America or Hollywood with the knowledge that I have of film and marketing and dealing with corporate, I probably would have fared better,” Chan said. “I was too young then, too naive.”

Asked later by an audience member how he navigates censorship in mainland China, Chan said: “Dealing with a corporate is very, very difficult. And if I can survive that, I can survive anything.” He added that limitations of budget, stars, studios or censorship tend to push filmmakers to be more creative.

After Hollywood, Chan set up Applause Pictures, a pan-Asian venture that made 10 films in two and a half years, most of them horror. Its output included “The Eye” franchise and the “Three” horror omnibus films, which brought together directors including Park Chan-wook, Miike Takashi, Kim Jee-woon and Fruit Chan. He also executive produced “One Fine Spring Day” for Korean director Hur Jin-ho – director of SGIFF opener “The Assassin(s)” – whose debut “Christmas in August” he loved. But a planned three-part love story with Hur and Japan’s Iwai Shunji found no investors.

“If we continue this pan-Asian effort, I’m going to be stuck with making horror films my whole life,” Chan said of the decision to move on to mainland China, where his first film was the 2005 musical “Perhaps Love.”

An aspiring screenwriter in the audience asked how he handles a scene that isn’t landing. “I don’t usually fix it for them. I make them fix it over and over and over and over again,” Chan said, adding that after saying “great” to everything at home, he doesn’t do the same with his writers.

He credited nine writers on “The Warlords,” and said screenwriters joke that his films’ writers would not fit in a minibus. “I milk the writer to death, and then I milk another writer,” he said. “So the writers’ community really don’t like me very much. But making movies is not about being well-liked.”

Though he is often seen as a genre-hopper, Chan said the same concerns run through his work, citing the love triangles in his debut “Alan & Eric: Between Hello and Goodbye,” “Comrades,” “Perhaps Love” and even “The Warlords,” which he called a love triangle between three brothers.

“Making every movie is answering some sort of life questions that I have at that stage, in point of my life,” he said. “So in a way, I’ve been making the same movie in my mind in the last 36 years.”

translated_excerpt_zh: 著名的亚洲电影制片人Peter Chan Ho-sun,导演的“朋友:几乎一个爱情故事”和“战士”,他说他可能会使用人工智能在他的电影制作,但“定义不是AIGC”,或人工智能创建的内容,而这两个小时的功能将保持其基础,反对短形的内容。

A Fermata in Venice: Reconfiguring the Rhythms of the Everyday

In the Hong Kong Collateral Event “Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice” at the 61st Venice Biennale, Hong Kong artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui rediscover the quiet rhythms of the everyday through new site-specific installations.

Amongst the bustle of the Venice Biennale, the Hong Kong Collateral Event turns to a quieter register. Curated by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA), Hong Kong’s first public art museum, the exhibition “Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice” marks the museum’s first curatorial undertaking for the Hong Kong exhibition at the Venice Biennale. Comprising five site-specific installations by artists Kingsley Ng and Angel Hui, the exhibition unfolds as a resonant journey rather than a series of isolated encounters, foregrounding the quotidian and the understated with a renewed attention.

Portrait of KINGSLEY NG (left) and his artwork Laundry Nocturne , 2026, and ANGEL HUI (right) and her artwork I Would Like to Open a Window for You , 2026. Courtesy Hong Kong Museum of Art.

The exhibition borrows fermata as its title and curatorial concept. In a musical score, it marks a moment of suspension, where a note or rest is prolonged at the performer’s discretion. In the Venetian cityscape, a fermata is a vaporetto stop—a threshold where passengers momentarily alight and embark. Resonating with the theme “In Minor Keys” of Venice Biennale 2026, the exhibition explores poetic rhythms in everyday life. Drawing on familiar yet fleeting moments in Hong Kong that subtly resemble those of Venice, the exhibition brings two cities into dialogue through shared conditions of everyday experience. Rooted in sensibilities shaped by Hong Kong, Ng and Hui bring distinct artistic approaches to a shared journey of self-discovery within the flow of life.

The fermata begins in the courtyard with Kingsley Ng. Ng is an established artist whose multimedia and spatial interventions often transform the familiar and the ethereal into meditative environments. Evolved from earlier renditions, his three installations for Venice trace his impressions between Venice and Hong Kong, attuning visitors to the overlooked rhythms of urban life. Sometimes, There Are Clouds in Puddles comprises mechanically triggered dichroic ribbons that reflect sunlight, creating the illusion of rain falling into five translucent, turquoise pools. Inspired by a poem by the late Hong Kong poet Leung Ping-kwan (Yasi), the work captures the fleeting magic of a rainy day.

This quiet observation continues indoors with Sky Well , where soap bubbles rotate within a hemispherical structure inspired by the spatial archetypes of wells in Hong Kong and Venice, as a single bulb sways above. The light is duplicated across the concave surface, creating an optical illusion that evokes an imagined cosmos and an image of impermanence.

KINGSLEY NG ,

Laundry Nocturne , 2026, dimensions variable. Courtesy Hong Kong Museum of Art.

Ng’s final installation, Laundry Nocturne , revisits the everyday ritual of drying laundry, a common sight across Hong Kong and Venice. A projected silhouette of a lone sheet sways under moonlight, accompanied by field recordings of Hong Kong’s night-time labour, from newspaper printing and sewage treatment to teahouses preparing for the day ahead. Gently bridging time zones, the sounds of nocturnal Hong Kong are carried into daytime Venice, as a tribute to the unseen labour. Across three installations, Ng reinterprets his impressions of Venice and observations of Hong Kong through humble materials, appreciating the everyday acts of maintenance that sustain urban life.

Alongside Ng’s immaterial approach, Angel Hui offers a tactile and sensory counterpoint through a practice grounded in material experimentation, daily objects and traditional artistic language. Known for her signature series of plastic bag embroidery, Hui, in her Venice debut, continues to transform the utilitarian into object for contemplation through traditional craftsmanship.

ANGEL HUI ,

I Would Like to Open a Window for You , 2026, dimensions variable. Courtesy Hong Kong Museum of Art.

Envisioned as one holistic spatial intervention, Hui’s two installations Drifting Sanctuary and I Would Like to Open a Window for You , span across two rooms as an imagined sanctuary, synchronised through light, sound and movement. In Drifting Sanctuary , plastic bags commonly used in Hong Kong to carry pet fish are stitched with goldfish motifs using traditional Suzhou embroidery technique, gently floating and flickering overhead. The shadows of the fish move across walls, drawing the gaze towards I Would Like to Open a Window for You , a slowly rotating wrought-iron window decorated with patterns characteristic to Hong Kong and Venice hand-crafted by Hui in collaboration with Hong Kong master artisans. The boundary between the two installations dissolves as the patterned silhouette of the window frame is cast across the rooms. Experienced as one immersive space, the two installations guide visitors towards Hui’s everyday observations in which overlooked objects hold care and delicate beauty.

The exhibition is neither a retreat nor a withdrawal from daily occurrences, but an invitation to linger with the familiar. Nestled in an old Venetian building opposite the main entrance of the Arsenale, “Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice” gives the uneventful everyday a moment to pause, remain and begin again.

Jointly presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department and the Hong Kong Arts Development Council (HKADC), and jointly organised by the Hong Kong Museum of Art (HKMoA) and the HKADC, the Hong Kong Collateral Event “Fermata: Hong Kong in Venice”, curated by the HKMoA, is currently on view in Venice (Campo della Tana, Castello 2126, 30122) through 22 November 2026.

Danny Trejo , who sparked backlash after it was revealed he’d be starring in the pro-ICE movie “ Pawn Shop ” from Ben Shapiro ’s production company, Daily Wire, had “never heard” of the conservative political commentator and is contractually unable to say anything negative about Shapiro — or the project — his son, Gilbert Trejo, said.

Gilbert shared a post to his Instagram story responding to the outcry from fans of the actor over the weekend, addressing claims that Danny is pro-ICE or supports Shapiro’s politics. He began by saying that only two weeks into shooting the project did any of the cast learn that Shapiro was involved, and that this father “has never heard of Ben Shapiro.” “I had to explain to him who that is, and what kind of guy he is,” wrote Gilbert.

He went on to write that Danny is unable to “badmouth” Shapiro or the film contractually. He also can’t “walk away without being sued for breach of contract. He couldn’t even release the statement he wanted to.” (Danny had previously told TMZ that he is a “proud Mexican who has always been and will always be a supporter of my community. I am also obviously pro-immigrant. I am not pro-ICE.. I know where I come from and I know our struggles. I am an actor. My job is to tell a story.”)

“It’s fucked up,” he continued. “He’s handcuffed to this stupid project, and swaths of people have instantly turned their back on him without knowing any of the facts.”

He said his father’s agent described the film as a “complicated story about a complicated time, where everyone looks bad except you, the hardworking Mexican shop owner who just wants peace,” to which Danny “jumped” at the idea of playing “a good guy.”

The logline for the film reads: “When a Minneapolis riot forces a young ICE officer to complete a high-stakes arrest alone after his partner is killed, he is hunted through the streets by a furious mob intent on freeing the prisoner and punishing anyone who still upholds the law. Barricaded inside a neighborhood pawn shop with a hard-edged Hispanic veteran and the man’s progressive college-age grandson, ordinary men must choose between the rule of law and the chaos that wants to burn it all down in a modern siege of honor and defiance.”

Read Gilbert’s full statement here.

For anyone seeing this shit with my dad…

He was booked on a film, it’s not pro-ice, its not overtly pro anything. His agent described it as ‘a complicated story about a complicated time, where everyone looks bad except you, the hardworking Mexican shop owner who just wants peace.”

He jumped at the idea of playing a good guy.

About 2 weeks into shooting everyone, including us, found out Ben Shapiro was involved.

My 82 year old dad has never heard of Ben Shapiro, I had to explain to him who that is, and what kind of guy he is.

My dad contractually can’t badmouth him, the film, or walk away without being sued for breach of contract. He couldn’t even release the statement he wanted to.

It’s fucked up. He’s handcuffed to this stupid project, and swaths of people have instantly turned their back on him without knowing any of the facts.

Ben Shapiro got Mexicans to abandon one of their heroes, got his own name to the top of google searches, and made us look like angry fools lacking any nuance. He wins.

article_text:
Source: Warner Bros

‘The Batman: Part II’

Inward spend on films shot in the UK took a hit in the first three quarters (Q1-3) of 2026, dropping by 40% year-on-year, but co-production was up by 31%.

The combined film and high-end TV production spend in the UK from January to September was £4.1bn, a 25.5% drop from 2025’s £5.5bn and 13% decrease from £4.7bn in 2024, according to figures published by the British Film Institute (BFI).

“The figures are the result of a complex picture, ranging from significant shifts in the global industrial context through to increased competitiveness from other international territories, and set against a backdrop of a strong Q1-3 period in 2025,” said a BFI spokesperson, with big projects to shoot last year including Amazon MGM’s Masters Of The Universe: Revolution , Sony’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day and HBO series House Of The Dragon and Harry Potter.

Overall film production spend was down 37% in Q1-3 2026 to £1.3bn from £2bn in the equivalent first reported period in 2025. However, the number of films starting production was 123, three more than first reported for Q1-3 2025.

Inward investment productions in Q1-3 2026 generated £1.1bn, or 87% of the total. A total of 36 inward investment films started production in this period, including Warner Bros’ The Batman: Part II and Universal’s The Mummy: Book Of The Dead in Q3. It is also down on the 2024 figure of £1.6bn spend on inward invesment films.

Last year, the third quarter was boosted by several big-budget US studio shoots in the UK, including Disney’s Star Wars: Starfighter , Amazon MGM Studios’ The Thomas Crown Affair and Warner Bros’ Clayface .

“This is obviously something we and the British Film Commission are looking at very closely,” added the BFI spokesperson. “We know the UK production sector delivers at scale, and few territories can compare to the depth of skill, creativity and productivity of our world-class workforce and talent, and we are looking forward to a number of large-scale productions scheduled for Q4 and 2027.”

Inward investment shoots plotted for the rest of this year include Paramount+’s Mobland season three and Hulu’s Mosquito. Projects on track to shoot in 2027 include Netflix’s Dog Fight , HBO’s House Of The Dragon season four and Amazon MGM’s Lord Of The Rings: The Rings Of Power season four.

Local production dips

Source: Dean Rogers

‘Mars Express’

Spend on local UK features in Q1-3 2026 was also down by 17%. Indigenous UK productions accounted for £103m (8% of the total) in the first three quarters.

UK films to shoot in Q3 included Mackenzie Crook’s Mars Express for Altitude and Big Talk Studios, Euros Lyn’s Pijin for Welsh-language broadcaster S4C and Edem Kelman’s Chairman produced by Two by Two Productions and Good Chaos.

Co-production spend was £68m (5% of the total) across Q1-3. Lineage , directed by Yann Demange, is a UK-France-Belgium that began shooting in the UK in Q3, with Crab Apple Films and Wayward producing out of the UK.

High-end TV

UK spend on high-end TV (HETV) programmes starting principal photography during Q1-3 2026 was £2.8bn from 133 productions. The number of programme starts was down 4% on first reported figures for Q1-3 2025 while spend was down 20%.

Inward investment programmes accounted for 79% of UK TV spend and 49% of programme starts in Q1-3 2026. Compared with first reported figures for Q1-3 2025, spend on inward investment programmes was down 23% with three fewer production starts in Q1-3 2026.

Inward investment HETV productions starting principal photography in Q3 2026 included HBO’s First Day On Earth , Apple’s The Husbands , Netflix’s Black Mirror season eight and FX’s Far Cry.

Local UK programmes accounted for 18% of spend and 43% of programmes, and co-productions for 3% of spend and 8% of programmes. Spend on local UK programmes was down 8% with five fewer production starts. BBC’s Hercule series one and Nightsleeper series two, ITV’s Code Zero and UKTV’s Bergerac series three started shooting in Q3.

Co-production spend was up 38% with three additional programme starts.

UK spend on feature-length single productions – including inward investment and local UK projects financed by broadcasters and streaming platforms – may be captured in the statistics for HETV, as these productions can apply for certification to access the UK’s HETV tax relief if they are unable to express theatrical intention.

The BFI presents the 2025 figures as ‘first reported’ to enable like-for-like comparisons; however, production data tends to be revised upwards throughout the year owing to lags in reporting from some productions, especially for local UK features with budgets of less than £500,000.

How France overhauled investment infrastructure and tax rebate in bid to woo large scale film and TV projects

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Hollywood action vet Renny Harlin is attached to direct rescue thriller Evac which will see a chopper crash-land in a volatile prison yard.

Evac will follow “a medical specialist who must team up with a wounded inmate she was sent to rescue after their medical helicopter crash-lands in a volatile prison yard. Together, the mismatched duo must survive the night and fight their way out amidst a dangerous, unfolding prison conspiracy.”

Written by Sidney King ( Skyfire ), the project is being produced by Michael Roccio ( Human Capital ), Robert Dean ( Trap House ) for uStudios, and producing partners Dawn Bursteen and Alan B. Bursteen of Milestone Studios, whose credits include the action-thriller Hunting Season and the upcoming horror film Invertigo , starring Inde Navarrette.

Related Stories

'The Beast's Renny Harlin & Keith Kjarval Reteaming On Action Thriller 'Athina'

Thunder Road, Renny Harlin & Aaron Eckhart Team On "'80s Throwback" Action Pic 'Trial By Combat' -- AFM

Casting discussions are under way with filming aimed at 2027.

Watch on Deadline

Cliffhanger and Die Hard 2 filmmaker Harlin most recently directed The Beast with Samuel L. Jackson, shark thriller Deep Water with Aaron Eckhart and Ben Kingsley, and Lionsgate’s horror trilogy The Strangers . “The script by Sidney King is a non-stop adrenaline rush,” said Harlin today. “It combines an intense, ticking-clock rescue mission with deep, character-driven stakes. The moment that chopper goes down, the audience will be trapped right there in the yard with our heroes. I’ve always loved high-octane stories where everyday professionals are thrown into extraordinary, survival-stakes environments.”

Producer Michael Roccio added: “We are thrilled to have Renny Harlin directing Evac . He is a true master of cinematic suspense and grand-scale action. Sidney has crafted a brilliant pressure-cooker world that balances prison politics with raw survival prowess. We are confident EVAC will become an unforgettable theatrical experience for action fans worldwide.”

Harlin is repped by M3 Global Strategy.

Film Review

Artavazd Pelechian’s Distant Connections

Through his “distance montage” technique, the Armenian filmmaker’s masterpieces are built around impressions, not stories.

We (1969), directed by Artavazd Pelechian, (all images courtesy New York Film Festival)

Artavazd Pelechian said his piece, and his admirers have waited decades for the world to take notice. The Armenian filmmaker, active primarily during the Soviet era, has a concise oeuvre : 13 works, mostly shorts, with two features that barely crack an hour. Aside from 2019’s Nature , he has not released anything since 1994. International recognition came gradually, but it has grown enough that many of his films have received 4K restorations that premiered at different festivals over 2026. Recently, the Pelechian Project was showcased at the New York Film Festival (NYFF), with eight of the director’s restored works in the program.

At the storied All-Union State Institute of Cinematography in Moscow in the 1960s, Pelechian and his peers studied the work of titanic Soviet directors like Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, and Dziga Vertov, who shaped cinematography and editing in cinema’s early days. Pelechian deviated from their example, developing an approach he described as “distance montage.” All his movies are montage-based, with intricate shot assemblages unified by distinct themes. Speaking with Scott MacDonald in the 1990s, Pelechian explained the distinction between distance montage and the familiar notion of a montage:

In Eisenstein, every element means something. For me, the individual fragments don’t mean anything anymore. Only the whole film has the meaning. … Eisenstein saw editing as a means to get from here to there , [whereas] I see editing as a means for seeing where we are .

The Seasons (1975), directed by Artavazd Pelechian

article_text:
「世界遺産の歩き方展」が2027年3月6日（土）から5月16日（日）まで寺田倉庫 G1ビル（東京・天王洲）にて開催されます。 本展は、海外旅行のバイブル『地球の歩き方』と放送30周年を迎えた『世界遺産』（TBS）が初めてタッグを組んだ、世界遺産の魅力と旅する楽しさを体験できる大型展覧会です。

1979年の創刊以来、世界約160の国と地域の魅力を届けてきた『地球の歩き方』。そして、1996年の放送開始以来、30年にわたって世界遺産の美しい映像を撮影してきた『世界遺産』（TBS）。知と映像が融合し、世界を見て、学んで、体感する旅が始まります。

会場では、空から世界遺産を巡るここでしか味わえない映像体験や、『地球の歩き方』の世界に入り込んで世界遺産の知識や雑学を学ぶ展示、異国の文化や暮らしに触れられるエリア、最新のVRで世界遺産を体験できる特別企画など、多彩なコンテンツを展開。高精細な大迫力の映像を通して、世界遺産の壮大なスケールと現地の空気感を体感できる没入型シアターも要注目です。また、世界を取材してきた番組制作スタッフやガイドブック編集者たちの知られざる舞台裏にも迫ります。

会場を出る頃には、“次に行きたい世界遺産”がきっと見つかるはずです。いつもの旅では出会えない「世界の奥行き」に触れる、かつてない“世界遺産を体感する”展覧会。さあ、一日で世界遺産を巡る旅へ出発しましょう！

2027年1月より、お得な前売チケットが販売開始予定。今後も、展示の追加情報やチケットの詳細、展覧会オリジナルグッズなど、さらなる情報が公開予定です。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

article_text:
連続テレビ小説「ブラッサム」で、いきなり大食漢ぶりを発揮して主人公の珠（石橋静河）を驚かせた黒崎大三郎。文壇の実力者です。この役を演じる遠藤憲一さんのコメントが届きました。

＜役柄＞黒崎大三郎 日本屈指の文芸雑誌「首都公論」を率いる編集長。豪胆な性格と鋭い審美眼で文壇を牽引する存在。

「個性の強い役でうれしく」

Q1 出演が決まったときの感想を教えてください。 遠藤さん ホームドラマ自体が好きなのでまた朝ドラに出たいと思っていました。でも1984年に『ロマンス』、2010年に『てっぱん』、2017年に『わろてんか』と３作出て、ヒロインの父親役も続いたのでもう来ないかなと。さすがに今回は父親役ではありませんでしたが、黒崎という個性の強い役が来てうれしかったです。NHK大阪放送局に来たのは『わろてんか』以来約10年ぶり。全部覚えているようでやっぱり忘れちゃってました（笑）

作家の才能を見抜く鋭さ

Q2 演じられる黒崎大三郎はどんな役ですか？ 遠藤さん 黒崎は最初から大食いのシーンがあって、大きな声でよく笑うダイナミックな人。その勢いを出しつつ、作家の才能を見抜く能力にたけた鋭さや心の中の純度の高さというギャップを表現できたらいいなと思いました。きっと１行読めば作品のよしあしがわかるほど、研ぎ澄まされた感性を持っているのでしょうね。だから熱意を買って受け取った珠（石橋静河）の原稿のさわりを読んだだけで、才能を感じたはずです。原石に出会うことが黒崎にとって一番の喜びだろうし、当時は女性作家もあまりいないので、実は誰よりも珠に期待しているのが厳しい言葉の中に感じられました。

僕自身は黒崎のようにまっすぐグイグイ来る人、好きです。ズバズバ言うけれどもアイデア豊富な編集長だから、作家たちもエネルギーがもらえて霧が晴れるような気分になるんじゃないかな。 ただ、「首都公論」がいい結果を生んでこられたのは、直感でワッと行くタイプの黒崎と冷静な分析ができてきっちり理論で後押ししてくれる副編集長・山中（井浦新）の二人三脚だったから。山中役の井浦君とは過去に一度共演していますが、常に清潔感のある人です。穏やかな物言いの中に力があるところが昔から変わらなくてすてきですね。

「ここが黒崎、というポイントのシーン」

Q3 黒崎大三郎を演じるうえで、印象に残っているシーンは？ 遠藤さん 1番初めに珠に原稿の感想を伝えるシーン（第5週 第24回）は大事に演じたかったし、自分の中で探って探って探りまくったとても印象的なシーンです。珠自身もあそこまで強く言われるとは思っていなかっただろうし、本当にこれでいいかな、でもやっぱりこれだなと思ったシーンですね。黒崎はストレートにすごいと言わず、あえて足りないものを見つけて本人に思いきりぶつけます。まずはここが黒崎という役の大きなポイントだと思って演じました。

珠は「相当に勇気のある生き方をしている」

Q4 『ブラッサム』の見どころや視聴者の皆さんへのメッセージをお願いします。 遠藤さん 珠ほど波乱万丈な主人公は、朝ドラになかなかいないと思います。それゆえのテンポの速さも『ブラッサム』の楽しみのひとつだろうし、当時としては相当勇気のある生き方をしているところが最大の見どころじゃないかな。朝ドラの新風という感じがします。この新しい風をぜひとも楽しんでほしいです。黒崎はとにかく生き急いでいる人ですが、仕事に対してはものすごくまっすぐ。これはどんな時代にも通じる大切なことなので、ご覧の皆さんにも伝わるといいなと思います。朝にしてはクセの強い役ですが、そういった部分も含めて楽しんでもらえたらうれしいです。 (美術展ナビ編集班)

article_text:
A celebrity preacher who performs daredevil stunts for his congregation while hiding his fixation on a young follower sits at the center of “ Trinity ,” the new feature from director Boo Junfeng , which is among the projects at this year’s Tokyo Gap-Financing Market .

Structured in three chapters modeled on the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, the film follows Johnny, a pastor from Taiwan whose sermons have built him a large Singaporean following at a popular megachurch. The faithful also turn out in large numbers for the elaborate acrobatic shows he stages in the vein of Cirque du Soleil.

Related Stories

‘60 Minutes’ Audience Sinks to Surprising Low Without Football

Though publicly known for his conservative stance, Johnny grows infatuated with Yang, a newcomer to his training program, and his preferential treatment of the young man soon becomes hard to miss. It unsettles his wife Ruth, and David, his leading disciple and his daughter’s husband-to-be, both of whom share in running the church.

When Yang vanishes, a frantic Johnny starts his own inquiry. The clues point toward the people in his inner circle, with tragic results. Johnny and Ruth later relocate to rural Taiwan, where they keep a low profile and worship at a modest local congregation – until Johnny glimpses an enigmatic stranger who may yet bring the couple divine grace.

“I’ve always been very interested in the subject of sexuality and faith, and I wanted to make a film that dives deep into the psyche of these characters within a church,” Boo said.

Boo, a Singaporean filmmaker, made his feature debut with “Sandcastle” (2010), which became the first film from Singapore to be selected for Cannes Critics’ Week. His follow-up, capital punishment drama “Apprentice,” played in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section in 2016. He has also served as creative director of Singapore’s National Day Parade, including the 2025 edition marking the country’s 60th anniversary, and currently serves as chair of the Singapore International Film Festival.

Producer Raymond Phathanavirangoon, whose credits include “Apprentice,” co-wrote “Trinity” with Boo and has been involved since the idea first took shape. He has also produced Pen-ek Ratanaruang’s “Headshot,” Ron Howard’s “Thirteen Lives” and Pang Ho-Cheung’s “Dream Home” and “Aberdeen.” His earlier career included stints as an international programmer for the Toronto International Film Festival and a program delegate for Cannes Critics’ Week, and he co-founded the Southeast Asia Fiction Film Lab (SEAFIC).

“Personally, I have had people close to me convert to Christianity due to Evangelism, but this is seldom seen in Asian films,” Phathanavirangoon said.

He added that the way some Asian churches build spectacle into their services is what sets the story apart. “Some are surprised that churches can host Cirque du Soleil-style performances like in our film, but just earlier this year in Korea, a stunt sent a man dressed as Jesus into the sky, and that went super viral.”

“Trinity” is now in post-production. Both Boo and Phathanavirangoon said the team is coming to Tokyo with a small gap in its financing left to close before the film can be completed.

“I hope people will empathize with the characters, despite them being flawed human beings,” Boo said.

The project is produced by Peanut Pictures, Filmagic Pictures and Gaïjin, and is listed as a co-production spanning 11 countries: Taiwan, France, Singapore, Poland, Greece, Japan, Germany, Brazil, South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines.

The Tokyo Gap-Financing Market runs as part of TIFFCOM, the content market attached to the Tokyo International Film Festival .

article_text:
Films and events

Cult

The Blood Countess

Die BlutGräfin

Isabelle Huppert dazzles as the Blood Countess in this delightful and high-camp gothic fantasy from visionary filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director-screenwriter Ulrike Ottinger

With Isabelle Huppert, Birgit Minichmayr, Thomas Schubert

Austria-Luxembourg-Germany 2026. 119min

Courtesy of MAGNIFY

Languages German, French With English subtitles

Introduction

After awakening from a long slumber, the Blood Countess embarks on a quest, with her devoted maid and trusty pet bat in tow, to search for an ancient text that could cause the demise of her vampire realm. Based on the legend of Countess Elizabeth Báthory, Huppert perfectly embodies the role of the bloodthirsty seductress who reigns over present-day Vienna.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

The Face of Horror

In this stunning, blood-soaked homage to Technicolor horror films, a woman in medieval England rises from the grave to wreak revenge on her husband.

Hot Spot

The new film from the acclaimed director of The Silent Twins is a daring and distinctive sci-fi thriller set in a near-future society ruled by sentient AI.

Queens of the Night: Female Vampires on Screen

Step into the seductive, dangerous and ever-evolving world of cinema's most captivating immortal: the female vampire.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在鹿特丹的梅利艺术研究所（Kunstinstituut Melly），南非艺术家莫谢夸·兰加（Moshekwa Langa）的展览“你会我们在最好的地方找到”（You Will Find Us in the Best Places）汇集了近120件作品，探讨了记忆、身份以及时间和地点之间不断变化的关系。[……]
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "在鹿特丹的梅利艺术研究所（Kunstinstituut Melly），南非艺术家莫谢夸·兰加（Moshekwa Langa）的展览“你会我们在最好的地方找到”（You Will Find Us in the Best Places）汇集了近120件作品，探讨了记忆、身份以及时间和地点之间不断变化的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moshekwa_detail_1__3-1030x692.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们该如何绘制一幅由流动、记忆和想象力塑造的人生图景？在展览“你会我们在最好的地方找到”（You Will Find Us in the Best Places）中，南非艺术家莫谢夸·兰加（Moshekwa Langa）通过他迄今为止在荷兰举办的最全面的展览，回顾了其长达三十年的艺术实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览占据了梅利艺术研究所（Kunstinstituut Melly）的全部4层空间，呈现了创作于1995年至2026年间的作品。兰加跨足绘画、拼贴、摄影、录像和装置等多种媒介，将日常生活材料、收集的物品以及个人经验的碎片转化为多层构图，模糊了现实与想象之间的界限。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在南非从种族隔离过渡的时期崭露头角，兰加发展出了一种获得国际认可的艺术实践，抵制关于身份和归属感的固定叙事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览由加比·恩戈博（Gabi Ngcobo）和卡贝洛·马拉齐（Kabelo Malatsie）策展，通过反复出现的理念而非严格的年表来切入他的作品，揭示了记忆、地点和未竟的叙事如何不断浮现。从他早期对国际双年展的参与，到对物质和记忆持续进行的探索，兰加的实践为理解时间和经验提供了另一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览“你会我们在最好的地方找到”（You Will Find Us in the Best Places）邀请观众走入一个历史交织、起点开放且意义不断被重构的艺术世界。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览将于2026年10月24日至2027年3月28日在鹿特丹的梅利艺术研究所（Kunstinstituut Melly）展出。", "links": [{"text": "Kunstinstituut Melly", "url": "https://www.kunstinstituutmelly.nl/en/people/9668-moshekwa-langa"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
At Kunstinstituut Melly in Rotterdam, South African artist Moshekwa Langa’s ‘You Will Find Us in the Best Places’ brings together nearly 120 works that explore memory, identity, and the shifting relationships between time and place.

How do we map a life shaped by movement, memory and imagination? In ‘You Will Find Us in the Best Places’, South African artist Moshekwa Langa reflects on three decades of artistic practice through his most comprehensive exhibition in the Netherlands to date.

The exhibition occupies all four floors of Kunstinstituut Melly and presents works created between 1995 and 2026. Working across drawing, collage, photography, video and installation, Langa transforms everyday materials, collected objects and fragments of personal experience into layered compositions that blur the boundaries between reality and imagination.

Emerging during South Africa’s transition from apartheid, Langa developed an internationally recognised practice that resists fixed narratives of identity and belonging.

Curated by Gabi Ngcobo and Kabelo Malatsie, the exhibition approaches his work through recurring ideas rather than strict chronology, revealing how memories, places and unfinished narratives continually resurface. From his early participation in international biennials to his ongoing explorations of material and memory, Langa’s practice offers alternative ways of understanding time and experience.

‘You Will Find Us in the Best Places’ invites audiences to encounter an artistic world where histories overlap, beginnings remain open, and meaning is continually reconstructed.

This exhibition will be on view at Kunstinstituut Melly in Rotterdam from 24 October 2026 until 28 March 2027.

article_text:
More than 30 years later after she blew away Street Fighter fans as bazooka-toting Cammy, Kylie Minogue nearly returned for a cameo in the latest feature adaptation.

The 2x Grammy-winning Australian pop icon’s friend and collaborator Orville Peck , who stars as Vega in the newly released Paramount video game movie, revealed that he “was trying to orchestrate” her return, but scheduling conflicts ultimately stood in the way.

“They were trying to get Kylie to do a cameo in our Street Fighter,” he told Queerty . “They were having a hard time getting ahold of her or whatever, and I was like, ‘Guys, I can text her.’ So, I was trying to orchestrate this whole thing, and it didn’t work out with timing. She was gonna be so down to do it.”

Related Stories

‘Street Fighter’ Official Trailer Shows Off The Pic’s Big Swing At A Video Game Classic

Orville Peck Wraps ‘Street Fighter’ Filming In Australia: “Back To My Music”

Peck added, “But of course, I immediately told Kylie when I got cast. She told me how filming their Street Fighter was one of the most fun experiences of her life, and she was like, ‘I’m so excited for you to get to do that.'”

Watch on Deadline

The Mule artist said he’s “still trying to orchestrate” a meeting between Minogue and Mel Jarnson, who plays Cammy in the Kitao Sakurai-helmed adaptation of the Capcom game.

@queerty This week, Orville Peck makes the jump from country crooner to action star in Street Fighter. But he’s not the first icon of music to do so: Back in 1994, his friend & collaborator Kylie Minogue starred in the original big-screen adaptation of the video game, and he says he texted her immediately when he got the part. And he’s got some tea, too: Apparently they tried to get Kylie to make a cameo in this Street Fighter! While Orville reveals she was “so down to do it,” timing just didn’t align, but he’s still hoping to orchestrate a photo op with his movie’s Cammy—actress Mel Jarnson—or maybe leave the door open for something in a potential sequel. Regardless, Kylie told Orville filming the ‘94 Street Fighter was “one of the most fun experiences of her life,” and it sounds like he felt the same this go-around, especially because he was emboldened to bring his full self to the project, leaning into queer energy to his portrayal of the masked character Vega. For our full conversation with @orvillepeck about @streetfightermovie, his latest album MULE and more, head to the link in our bio. @kylieminogue queerty #orvillepeck #streetfighter #streetfightermovie #kylieminogue ♬ original sound – Queerty* – Queerty*

“Maybe the sequel, we’ll see,” teased Peck of a potential Minogue cameo.

In 2024, Peck featured Minogue and Diplo on his song “Midnight Ride”, released as a single on his third studio album Stampede .

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Éditions Odyssée 出版了《安妮·加德：目光地理》（Géographie du regard），这是一部与 MPP – 遗产与摄影多媒体图书馆（Médiathèque du patrimoine et de la photographie）合作制作的专著。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“对安妮而言，如果没有快门释放那一刻的奇妙魔法——通过奇特的化学反应，光线在胶片透明表面上转化为影像——那么照相机或大画幅相机、视点和构图的选择便毫无意义。正是通过掌握这些化学与光影的偶然性，安妮才走上了摄影之路。”——吉尔·德西雷·迪·戈塞（Gilles Désiré dit Gosset）与马修·里瓦兰（Matthieu Rivallin），MPP", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一位杰出的艺术家和技术专家，安妮·加德在当代摄影界占据着独特的位置。自1980年代以来，她一直在“居所摄影”与“增强摄影”的交汇处发展出自由不羁的作品系列，这种实践利用短暂的装置来揭示那些通常边缘化或不同寻常的场所。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在生活、写作和旅行伴侣劳尔·韦尔涅尔（Laure Vernière）的陪伴下，她随着委托和拍摄主题走遍世界。从中亚到中国，再到千面印度的过程中，她为爱马仕（Hermès）铺展出一根红丝线，拍摄了王公（mahajaras）与纳瓦卜（nawabs）的宫殿，以及巴西和纽约的当代建筑……", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "汲取了这些经历与色彩的养分，她以全新的目光审视了波尔多（她的故乡）的潜艇基地、大西洋海岸的碉堡、东京宫和夏约宫寂静的建筑，以及孟加拉国吉大港的造船厂——全球化的巨轮在那里被手工拆解。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如同旅行日志一般，这本专著重新梳理了这些摄影叙事的碎片与记忆。它追溯了一位艺术家的创作轨迹，她关注现实的痕迹、缺席与蜕变，正如记者兼作家皮埃尔·韦耶泰（Pierre Veilletet）所言，她的影像揭示了“美那受损的背面”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《安妮·加德：目光地理》（Anne Garde: Géographie du regard） Éditions Odyssée 出版社 责任编辑：卡米尔·加莱（Camille Gallet）与吉尔·卡格雷（Gilles Cargueray） 艺术指导：Studio Hudson Catty 前言：吉尔·德西雷·迪·戈塞与马修·里瓦兰（MPP） 文本：劳尔·韦尔涅尔等人 后记：伊丽莎白·韦德雷讷（Élisabeth Védrenne） 272页 17 × 24 cm（6.7 × 9.4 in） 325幅彩色及黑白摄影作品 平装 语言：法语 ISBN 978-2-494767-61-4 €44 http://www.editionsodyssee.com", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Éditions Odyssée publishes Anne Garde: Géographie du regard ( Geography of the Gaze ) , a monograph produced in partnership with the MPP – Médiathèque du patrimoine et de la photographie (Heritage and Photography Library).

“For Anne, the camera or view camera, the choice of viewpoint and framing count for nothing without the magic of the instant when, through a strange chemical reaction, light turns into an image on the transparent surface of the film as the shutter is released. It is through mastering these chemical and luminous chances that Anne came to photography.” – Gilles Désiré dit Gosset and Matthieu Rivallin MPP

An exceptional artist and technician, Anne Garde holds a singular place in the contemporary photographic landscape. Since the 1980s, she has developed a free-spirited body of work at the crossroads of an “inhabited photography” and an “augmented photography,” a practice that uses ephemeral installations to reveal places that are often marginal or unusual.

Alongside Laure Vernière, her partner in life, writing and travel, she travels the world where commissions and subjects take her. From Central Asia to China and on to India of a thousand faces, she unrolls a thread of red silk for Hermès and photographs the palaces of maharajas and nawabs, and contemporary architecture in Brazil and New York…

Nourished by these experiences and colors, she casts a renewed eye on the submarine base of Bordeaux (her native city), the bunkers of the Atlantic coast, the silent architecture of the Palais de Tokyo and the Palais de Chaillot, and also the shipyards of Chittagong in Bangladesh, where the great ships of globalization are dismantled by hand.

Like a travel notebook, this monograph rearranges the fragments and memories of these photographic narratives. It traces the path of an artist attentive to the traces, absences and metamorphoses of the real, whose images reveal, in the words of journalist and writer Pierre Veilletet, “the corrupted underside of beauty.”

article_text:
News

Vatican Exhibition Series Centers "Fundamentally Human" Art Over AI

A triennale across seven cities expands on Pope Leo XIV's message that artificial intelligence models “lack the affective, relational and spiritual perspective” necessary to create art.

An exhibition series organized by the Vatican brings together more than 100 artists — including Arthur Jafa, Jeremy Frey, and Mona Hatoum — to celebrate “ fundamentally human ” creativity in the face of AI's rapid rise.

Across seven coinciding international exhibitions, the Catholic Universities Art Triennale (ArtCut) centers empathy and self-reflection as the primary drivers of humanity's progress, rather than technological advancement. ArtCut's inaugural edition is assembled under the umbrella of Exercises in Empathy , expanding on Pope Leo XIV's earlier encyclical on safeguarding the human condition from AI's capacities for manipulation and delusional omnipotence.

Cardinal Tolentino de Mendonça, prefect of the Dicastery for Culture and Education of the Holy See, commissioned ArtCut's contemporary art exhibitions at seven Catholic universities across Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Italy, Portugal, Angola, and the United States.

The Triennale responds directly to the Pope's assertion that AI systems “do not understand what they produce, for they lack the affective, relational and spiritual perspective through which human beings grow in wisdom.” Within this framework, each exhibition focuses on defining facets of humanity, both physical and intellectual.

article_text: Every January, as we ring in the new year, we take a moment to take a look at some of the major new releases of the holiday season. This year, Film Comment Editors Devika Girish and Clinton Krute invited critics Beatrice Loayza and Mark Asch to focus on a select handful of titles that have recently graced the marquees of multiplexes, and which continue to stir up discourse. The group kicks things off with a deep dive into James Cameron’s latest 3D space opera, Avatar: Fire and Ash (4:00), before turning their attention to another epic, Josh Safdie’s Marty Supreme (33:34) —which both Beatrice and Mark have written great essays on in recent weeks. They also touch on James L. Brooks’s Ella McCay (51:15) , which Mark reviewed for Film Comment just last week.
